name: smart-pointer
intent: Give a heap object a handle type that behaves like a pointer but carries its ownership semantics, so the object's lifetime is decided by the type system - or by a documented protocol - instead of by scattered calls to free or delete.
problem: A raw pointer says where an object is but nothing about who owns it: release calls scatter across callers, one exit path forgets one and leaks, another releases twice, and a returned object has no stated owner; where ownership is genuinely shared, no component can say when the last user is done.
context: Applies to heap-allocated objects whose lifetime crosses function boundaries: factory results, polymorphic objects stored through base interfaces, shared graphs and caches, handle/body (pimpl) wrappers, and resources whose release must happen on every exit path including exceptions. It also applies when ownership spans threads (shared counting with atomics) or must be observed without being kept alive (weak references).
benefits: Ownership becomes a property of the type: a unique-ownership handle cannot be copied, so transfer is explicit and the compiler rejects the accidental aliasing behind double deletes; a shared handle makes the number of owners visible.
Release is deterministic and runs on every exit path - normal return, early return and exception - which raw new/delete cannot guarantee.
The handle delegates the pointee's interface (operator->, Deref, arrow-style access), so callers use the body directly instead of a duplicated wrapper API.
Non-owning edges are expressible separately (weak handles, borrowed raw pointers and references), so cycles and back-references stop keeping objects alive while staying observable.
Destruction policy is separated from the object: custom deleters and allocators adapt foreign resources (FILE*, OS handles, malloc'd buffers) to the same lifetime discipline.
tradeoffs: Shared ownership costs a control block and atomic counter traffic: an extra allocation per object and contention when handles cross threads; unique ownership avoids both but cannot be shared.
Reference counting cannot reclaim cycles: two shared handles pointing at each other leak until a weak edge breaks one direction, so the pattern adds a design obligation rather than removing one.

A weak or borrowed view can expire between the check and the use; concurrent code must promote it (weak_ptr::lock, Weak::upgrade) and handle the empty result, which is a failure mode raw pointers do not have.
Move-only handles propagate through APIs: copies are erased, so signatures become by-value moves and by-reference borrows, and moved-from values remain valid but unspecified.

Ownership is only as good as its discipline - adopting one raw pointer into two owning handles, or aliasing a smart pointer with a raw one, recreates double-free and use-after-free bugs; plain value semantics are often simply better than heap indirection.

participants.responsibility: Pointer-like value that owns the pointee: copy, move and destruction transfer ownership, adjust a count, or release the object; its size and access cost stay comparable to a raw pointer where the language allows.
The heap object whose lifetime is managed; it implements no lifetime logic itself and is normally unaware of how it is owned.
The destruction and deallocation strategy the handle applies at the end of ownership (delete, custom deleter, allocator, close function), kept separate from the pointee's own code.

Shared state holding the strong and weak counts plus the deleter; created once per object and referenced by every shared and weak handle, which is why a second control block for the same object corrupts ownership.
Non-owning view that does not keep the pointee alive and must be promoted or checked (lock, upgrade, TryGetTarget) before use; raw pointers and plain references are its manual equivalent.

use_cases: Factory and builder results: the factory returns the handle by value, so ownership transfer is part of the signature and no caller has to remember a delete.
Polymorphic collections: containers of owning handles keep derived objects alive without slicing and destroy them when the container goes away.
Shared graphs, caches and sessions where several components use the same object and its end of life is 'when the last user is done'; back edges are weak so the graph can actually be reclaimed.
Handle/body (pimpl, Cheshire Cat) wrappers whose header hides the body type: the handle owns the body and delegates access, replacing a duplicated interface or a manual delete.
Asynchronous operations that must keep their state alive: the task holds a shared or owning handle until it completes, while a weak handle lets the rest of the system detect that it is gone.
Wrapping non-memory resources (files, sockets, locks, native buffers) with a custom deleter, so the same discipline covers them.

C++ standard library: unique_ptr as the default single-owner handle, shared_ptr/weak_ptr for genuinely shared objects with one control block, and make_unique/make_shared as the creating factories; the C++ Core Guidelines codify this set (R.20, R.32-R.37) as the language's default resource-management style.

Rust standard library: Box for unique ownership, Rc for single-threaded shared ownership and Arc for handles that cross threads, Weak (Rc::downgrade/Arc::downgrade, promoted with upgrade) as the sanctioned cycle breaker; the borrow checker makes the owning-versus-borrowed split a compile-time property of every signature.

Swift: automatic reference counting turns every class reference into an owning handle with deinit at the last strong owner, and supplies the non-owning views - weak for a peer that may die first (nilled on deallocation) and unowned for an equal-or-longer-lifetime peer; delegate back edges, parent-child links and closure captures of self are the documented strong-reference cycles to break with them.
avoid_when: Plain value semantics suffice: an object that can live on the stack, in a container or inside another object should not be heap-allocated just to be 'managed'; add indirection only where it is needed.
The object's lifetime is exactly one lexical scope and no ownership transfer happens: a stack object or a scope guard is simpler and cannot leak.

The runtime is garbage-collected and offers no ownership types: hand-written owning wrappers or counts cannot control reclamation and fight the collector - use the runtime's references plus its weak and cleanup facilities (see the per-language notes).
Object graphs need cycle collection or arena-wide reclamation: reference counting leaks cycles, so a tracing collector or an arena/region owns the graph instead.
A framework already owns the lifetime (dependency-injection scopes, ORM sessions, pools): wrapping the object in your own owning handle duplicates or contradicts the container's teardown.
Interop-heavy hot paths where the control block and atomics are measured overhead: intrusive ownership or a value design removes the extra allocation.
anti_patterns: shared ownership everywhere 'to be safe': cycles leak, ownership stops being reviewable, and the atomic counter becomes contention on hot paths.
Constructing a second owning handle from a raw pointer that is already owned (shared_ptr(p.get()), double adopt) - two control blocks, one double free.
Naked new/delete or malloc/free in code that already has owning handles, so two lifetime disciplines coexist and reviewers cannot tell which pointer owns.
Wrapping every member in a smart pointer to avoid copying, turning a value object into a graph of heap allocations - pessimisation by indirection.
Dereferencing a weak or borrowed view without promoting it, or keeping the promoted pointer beyond the guarantee.
design_principles: Make illegal states unrepresentable: owning and non-owning references are different types, so the compiler or the API distinguishes them.
Single responsibility: the handle manages lifetime, the body manages behaviour, the deleter manages destruction policy.
RAII / deterministic cleanup: acquisition and release are tied to object lifetime, so every exit path releases.
Zero overhead where possible: unique ownership must add no runtime cost beyond the pointer; pay for sharing only where ownership is genuinely shared.
Least privilege for observers: code that only needs to look at an object receives a borrow, raw pointer or weak handle, not a share in its ownership.
best_practices: Default to unique ownership and upgrade to shared only where ownership is genuinely shared; hand out non-owning views (references, raw pointers, weak handles) from the owner.
Create owning handles through the language's factory (make_unique/make_shared, Box::new, Rc::new) or directly from the allocation; never build two owning handles for one raw pointer.
Express ownership in API signatures: by-value or move means 'takes ownership', reference or raw pointer means 'borrows', a weak handle means 'observes without keeping alive'.
Break every cycle deliberately with a weak handle, and document the ownership graph next to the types.
Keep handles small and pass them by reference when only observing; a shared counter is an atomic, not a free field.
Use custom deleters (or a small RAII wrapper) so non-memory resources are released by the same discipline, and prefer standard library handles to hand-rolled ones.
sources: Tyagi & Volchko (eds.), More C++ Idioms, Wikibooks - 'Smart Pointer' idiom: handle/body delegation with ownership smartness; known uses std::auto_ptr, boost::shared_ptr, CORBA Var types.
C++ Core Guidelines (ISO C++ foundation) - R.20/R.32-R.37 and F.7: express ownership in types, and do not pass a pointer or reference obtained from an aliased smart pointer.
GotW #91 Solution: Smart Pointer Parameters (Herb Sutter) - why passing shared_ptr/unique_ptr by value or reference when no ownership is intended is a pessimisation; take T* or T& to observe.
